question: According to the World Health Organization, how is an Adverse Drug Reaction (ADR) defined?

options.A: A predictable side effect that is always beneficial to the patient
options.B: A noxious and unintended response occurring at doses normally used in humans
options.C: Any unintended effect caused exclusively by an intentional medication overdose
options.D: A therapeutic failure resulting from a substandard counterfeit medication

explanation: The WHO defines an ADR as a noxious and unintended response to a medicine occurring at normal doses used for prophylaxis, diagnosis, or therapy. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h1)

question: What primary role do nurses play regarding adverse drug reactions in clinical practice?

options.A: Prescribing alternative medications to replace the offending drug
options.B: Manufacturing safer pharmaceutical alternatives for hospital use
options.C: Acting as a safety net through early recognition, monitoring, and reporting
options.D: Diagnosing the root pathophysiological cause of the adverse reaction

explanation: Nurses are on the frontline of medication administration and serve as a safety net by monitoring patients, recognizing ADRs early, and reporting them. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which characteristic best describes a Type A (Augmented) Adverse Drug Reaction?

options.A: It is completely unpredictable and immune-mediated
options.B: It is dose-dependent and predictable based on pharmacology
options.C: It occurs long after the drug therapy has been discontinued
options.D: It represents complete failure of the medication to work

explanation: Type A reactions are dose-dependent and predictable because they stem from the exaggerated pharmacological action of the drug. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h2)

question: What is the appropriate initial nursing and medical management for a Type B (Bizarre) ADR such as anaphylaxis?

options.A: Reduce the drug dose by half and monitor vital signs
options.B: Double the dose to build patient tolerance to the drug
options.C: Immediately discontinue the drug and ensure lifelong avoidance
options.D: Continue the medication while adding a prophylactic antihistamine

explanation: Type B reactions are unpredictable and severe, requiring immediate discontinuation of the drug and permanent avoidance to prevent recurrence. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h2)

question: How do pharmacokinetic mechanisms commonly contribute to adverse drug reactions?

options.A: By altering drug absorption, metabolism, or excretion, leading to drug accumulation
options.B: By blocking normal receptor sites to intentionally cause therapeutic failure
options.C: By triggering a Type I IgE-mediated immediate anaphylactic response
options.D: By causing genetically determined enzyme deficiencies in red blood cells

explanation: Pharmacokinetic mechanisms involve changes in ADME processes, which can cause the drug to accumulate in the body and result in toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h3)

question: What underlying mechanism causes hemolytic anemia in a G6PD-deficient patient given primaquine?

options.A: A predictable Type A pharmacological blood pressure drop
options.B: An idiosyncratic, genetically determined abnormal reaction to the chemical
options.C: A Type IV delayed contact dermatitis hypersensitivity reaction
options.D: An intentional overdose of the prescribed antimalarial medication

explanation: Reactions like G6PD deficiency-related hemolysis are idiosyncratic, meaning they are abnormal and genetically determined responses to a drug. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h3)

question: Why are older adults particularly susceptible to adverse drug reactions?

options.A: They have enhanced liver enzyme activity and rapid renal elimination
options.B: They experience physiological declines in renal and hepatic function alongside polypharmacy
options.C: They are completely immune to Type B idiosyncratic drug reactions
options.D: They lack cytochrome P450 enzymes entirely throughout their lifespan

explanation: Older adults have reduced organ function (renal and hepatic) and often take multiple medications (polypharmacy), increasing their risk for ADRs. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is a major risk factor associated with polypharmacy in clinical nursing practice?

options.A: Decreased likelihood of experiencing drug-drug interactions
options.B: Exponentially increased risk of drug interactions and cumulative toxicity
options.C: Complete elimination of genetic metabolic variations
options.D: Guaranteed patient compliance with all prescribed drug regimens

explanation: Taking multiple medications concurrently (polypharmacy) raises the risk of adverse drug-drug interactions and toxicity. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h4)

question: What is the 'prescribing cascade' in the context of adverse drug reactions?

options.A: Stopping all medications immediately when an allergy occurs
options.B: Misinterpreting an ADR as a new disease symptom and prescribing a new drug to treat it
options.C: Gradually tapering a medication dose to avoid withdrawal symptoms
options.D: Administering multiple incompatible drugs in a single intravenous line

explanation: The prescribing cascade occurs when an ADR is mistaken for a new medical condition, resulting in an unnecessary new prescription to treat the reaction. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h5)

question: Which action is a key component of clinical causality assessment for a suspected ADR?

options.A: Increasing the drug dosage to see if the symptoms become permanent
options.B: Evaluating the temporal relationship between drug administration and symptom onset
options.C: Ignoring baseline laboratory values and focusing solely on patient complaints
options.D: Immediately discharging the patient without further observation

explanation: Evaluating the time elapsed between starting the drug and the onset of symptoms is a fundamental step in determining if the drug caused the reaction. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h5)

question: What is the immediate priority nursing action when a severe ADR is identified in a hospitalized patient?

options.A: Increase the infusion rate of the suspected medication
options.B: Withhold or stop the offending medication and notify the physician
options.C: Wait for the scheduled pharmacy delivery time before taking action
options.D: Document the incident in the nursing notes at the end of the shift

explanation: The first step in managing any suspected ADR is to immediately stop the offending drug to prevent further exposure and notify the doctor. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which nursing intervention is most effective in preventing ADRs during care transitions?

options.A: Medication reconciliation to eliminate discrepancies and duplicate therapies
options.B: Administering all oral medications through an intravenous line instead
options.C: Avoiding patient education to prevent causing unnecessary anxiety
options.D: Relying solely on verbal medication histories provided by family members

explanation: Medication reconciliation across care transitions ensures accurate lists are maintained, preventing duplicate drugs and dosing errors. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which agency in Nigeria is primarily responsible for post-marketing surveillance and pharmacovigilance?

options.A: Nursing and Midwifery Council of Nigeria (NMCN)
options.B: National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control (NAFDAC)

explanation: NAFDAC is the regulatory body tasked with drug safety monitoring, post-marketing surveillance, and pharmacovigilance in Nigeria. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h7)

question: What is the primary tool traditionally used by healthcare professionals in Nigeria to report adverse drug reactions to NAFDAC?
explanation: NAFDAC utilizes the 'Yellow Form' for spontaneous reporting of adverse drug reactions by healthcare providers. [learn more](GNS215_U2_T5#GNS215_U2_T5_h7)
